<reason>Both sides executed at a high level and stayed on the motion. B's strongest work was collapsing the operational/reputational distinction ("What PRO calls stigma, a CFO calls counterparty risk"), catching A's concession on presentation controls, and the memorable "who spends the asset" framing, plus a bold, honest "Yes" to A's Q2 defended as brand stewardship. But A held the "solely" carve-out under sustained pressure: A's rejoinder that attaching a price tag to public hostility does not convert it into creator misconduct blunted B's collapse move, A answered B's pressure questions directly with a coherent enforceable design (no bailout, stated reasons, inability-to-settle as an independent operational ground), and A's Q1 reductio — hostile customers vetoing any unpopular lawful business — was answered by B only descriptively (freedom of contract, cannabis/payday precedent) rather than normatively. A's closing hit that gap precisely: "freedom of contract identifies who decides; it does not establish what they should decide." B also paid a minor cost for a clipped rebuttal 2. Narrow but real edge to A on the proposition as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over A's pressure Q2 and B's A2 answer: B bit the bullet that exclusion is justified even with perfect age-gating and no expected loss, framing it as stewardship of brand equity, while A's closing converted that admission into proof that B's rule protects a gateway's "preference not to be associated" rather than any operational interest — the sharpest and most decision-relevant clash of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
